s06t.slug: THURSDAY · 5:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — MEDIUM SPARKLE
body: The speakers on Theo’s sill are already going when Jack gets the door open with his elbow, the pie box out in front of him in both hands: a piano that finds one chord and keeps going back to it, patient as somebody knocking at a house with the lights on, and under it a drum machine that has all night. The sun is down in the eucalyptus. What is left of it comes through the one window and lies across 412 in a long orange slab, and in the slab, side by side on the two made beds, sit two bags.

They are quilted, pink and enormous, with grosgrain bows on the handles that look measured. Across the flap of each, on a strip of white label-maker tape, is a name. Theo’s says MR. THEODORE, MEDIUM SPARKLE. Jack’s says FIREMAN, LARGE.
Theo stands at the foot of the beds in his shirtsleeves with his hands clasped behind him, as at a viewing. Jack sets the pie on his desk, beside the mug.
“Close the door,” Theo says. “And witness.”
“Who brought them up?”

“Marcus, on the move-in cart. I didn’t ask what she paid him. I’m guessing a casserole and a look. She was up till two with the label maker.” He tilts his head at the floor. “I heard it through two floors. A very small typewriter that has been wronged.” His own bag sits untouched, with a kind of clearing around it. “I said I wouldn’t open it alone. A man shouldn’t be alone with a bag that knows his soul.”

He unzips it and takes out the first thing his hand finds: a black Saints T-shirt sequined from collar to hem in gold, which catches what is left of the window and throws it across the ceiling in a thousand small coins.
“Sequins,” Jack says.
“‘Medium,’” says Theo. “She was being modest.”

Under the shirt there is a hank of Mardi Gras beads in purple, green and gold, wound up like fishing line, and under that, folded in tissue as if it were evening wear, a black satin sleep mask. Theo lifts the mask out in both hands and holds it to the light.
“She knows my soul,” he says, quietly.

Jack opens FIREMAN, LARGE, and it is a different kind of document. Foam earplugs, sealed in pairs. An inflatable horseshoe pillow with its valve taped shut. A box of Dramamine. Three packs of gum in three flavors, as if flavor were an insurance policy. And an extra-large Saints T-shirt, plain black cotton, the fleur-de-lis printed flat, not a sequin on it anywhere.
“She spared you the sparkle,” Theo says. “Don’t mistake that for mercy. That’s tailoring.”
“Dramamine. I don’t get carsick.”
“She’s provided for your worst day, Costigan. Be moved.”
An index card is tucked into the pillow’s fold, written in a round hand that makes every period a small balloon.

body.title: An index card, inside the bag

body: Under the D there is a flourish you could hang a banner from.
“D,” Jack says.

“For Delaney. It’s how she signs a warning.” Theo folds the mask back into its tissue. “She sized you from the Commons steps with one eye shut and her thumb up, like a painter. I was asked to confirm. I confirmed.”

Jack’s own packing takes four minutes: the duffel from Glenwood Avenue, jeans, a week of socks that he suspects is optimistic, the rosary, and on top Hale’s old paperback of *The Moviegoer* with Hale’s pencil all down its margins. Theo’s takes the evening. The weekender lies open on the floor, camel leather with TAV across the flap in letters you could sign a treaty with, and he builds into it in ranks: shirts rolled and laid out by their likelihood of creasing, socks balled and sorted by temperament, the blazer folded in thirds with tissue in the lapels, the sequins set apart in a pillowcase of their own, in quarantine.
“It’s a weekend bag,” Jack says.
“It’s a bag with sequins in it. The sequins snag the wool, the wool pills the satin, and the beads have a grievance against everything. I have seated weddings with fewer landmines.”
On the nightstand Hollis sits in his teacup with a laminated card propped against the saucer in Priya Raman’s hand: CUSTODIAN: P. RAMAN, R.A. TERMS ATTACHED.

body.text: “You told me I’d never asked you for anything,” Theo says, to a sock. “I’ve been trying to decide all day if that was a compliment.” Jack starts to answer and is waved off with the sock.

body: “I didn’t thank you,” Theo says. He says it to the weekender. “For the text.”
“You asked.”
“I’m aware. I’m told it’s habit-forming.”
“How’s Callender?” he asks, between one sock and the next.
“Three suitcases and a crisis. I’m seeing her at nine-thirty.”
“Naturally.”

Theo takes the shirt he folded a minute ago out of the weekender, shakes it open, and folds it again: sleeves back, then in thirds, then once more than that. The piano goes around to its second chord and the drum machine comes in under it. Behind Jack, FIREMAN, LARGE sits open with its horseshoe pillow out, and Theo, on his knees on the floor, smooths the shirt flat on his thigh and does not put it in.

response: Theo stops. The shirt stays where it is.

“Don’t,” he says. “Okay? Just —” And he puts it in the weekender, on top of the pillowcase of sequins, which is the one arrangement he has spent the whole evening ruling out. He closes the flap on it.

The bag was finished at six. It takes Theo until five to eight to agree. Then he hands Jack FIREMAN, LARGE by its bows and reaches over and cuts the speaker in the middle of a bar, and the piano stops on a note, and the room has to hold its shape without it.

choices.text: *Put on the sleep mask and critique his folding.*
response: Jack lifts the mask out of its tissue, which is permitted because Theo is too surprised to prevent it, and pulls it down over his eyes. It is cool and slick and smells of Laney’s hand cream, gardenia, a Texas threat.
“The sleeves are amateur,” he says to the dark, and to roughly where Theo was. “The collar’s facing the wrong wall. I’m told there are socks, and I can only assume it’s a disaster.”
Theo laughs outright, and then, because he cannot help it, pitches it. “A blind man reviews a weekender. Rated R for linens. It’s an awards picture, Costigan. It opens in December.”

Jack keeps the mask on through the rest of the folding, on principle, issuing notes. At five to eight Theo’s hand finds the light switch and the room goes dark, and Jack, in satin, is the last person in it to find out. “We’re going down,” Theo says, and puts FIREMAN, LARGE into his hands by its bows.

choices.text: “Why do you need me there, Theo?”
response: Theo stops with a sock in each hand. “Because I asked,” he says.
That is the whole answer. He looks at it, and then he becomes absorbed in the weekender’s luggage tag, which he reads front and back, though there is nothing on it but his name.
At five to eight the mask goes into his blazer pocket, not the bag, where he can reach it. He lifts FIREMAN, LARGE off the bed and holds it out to Jack by its bows.
